title: Awe close
hookLine: fifty-six days of looking up; awe, the traditions agree, makes us humble, though they name its source differently

cards: Fifty-six days. This block opened with a plain question: what is awe?
Since then: Moses with his shoes off, a still small voice, the heavens declaring, Arjuna before the universal form, Pascal in infinite spaces, Emerson as a transparent eyeball.

Then outside: sunrises, clouds, one tree, water, storms, a newborn, a sacred building visited as a guest. And these last days, a heartbeat, a sink full of dishes, an eclipse, and four nights of wonder.
So what did it add up to?

teach.b: First, what kept happening. In story after story, awe made people smaller. Not crushed.
Smaller, the way a person can feel at the edge of the ocean. Second, the voice from the whirlwind, which asked Job about the stars on the night-sky day.
After Job has demanded answers for chapter after chapter, God finally speaks, and the first thing God does is ask a question.

In the King James words: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Job wanted an explanation. He's handed a question instead, and he comes out of it quiet.
In Job's story, and in the Jewish and Christian reading of it, the source of awe is God. Third, the poet in the field.

teach.h: I AM NOTHING; I SEE ALL.
teach.b: Emerson, standing on bare ground under an open sky, wrote: "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all".

In the same sentence he says the currents of the Universal Being circulate through him, and that he is part or particle of God: a God met in the woods and the open field, not a voice from a whirlwind.
Some of this block's scientists found the same smallness with no God named: in the age of the stars, the length of time, the size of what's out there. Fourth, what's easy to miss.
In these two, the smallness isn't the end.
Job is humbled, and then his story goes on. Emerson says he's nothing and, in the same breath, that he sees all. The traditions name the source differently, and they don't have to agree.
But in these stories, the people who felt awe came back lighter.
Smaller, and somehow glad to be.

how: Some Jews and Christians read the book of Job, including God's speech from the whirlwind, as a picture of awe before the Creator; some readers of Emerson and some people with no religious tradition also seek the same humbling in nature.

o: Arjuna's vision, one name this block gave awe's source
a single shape that every religion agrees God has
the shape of the universe as scientists measure it

games.q: you're Job. you've demanded answers for a long time, and finally God speaks out of the whirlwind. what comes first?
o: a point-by-point answer to your complaints.
a question: where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?
an apology for what you've suffered.
games.why: God opens with a question, not an explanation, and Job comes out of it quiet.

practice: Lift your eyes to the sky through a window, or to the highest point in the room, and let one moment from this block come back on its own: a line, a night, a sunrise, a heartbeat.
If you pray, give thanks to the source you believe in; if you don't, stay with the size of things, the smaller thing in the picture.
